How to reach US Hispanic customers with Meta ads (and judge it by CAC)

You cannot target by ethnicity on Meta, and a Spanish language setting misses many bilingual buyers. The answer is a structured creative test, measured in cost per paying customer.

Published November 26, 20268 min read

In this article

  1. Why there is no "Hispanic" audience on Meta
  2. The language setting trap
  3. How to set up Meta ads for US Hispanic customers: the three-version test
  4. Keep the language after the click
  5. Budget the test from your maximum CAC
  6. Read the results with total CAC, not media CAC

  9. Where a bilingual team helps

  11. Frequently asked questions
SeePaid media

Quick answer

To reach US Hispanic customers with Meta ads, do not rely on a Spanish language setting alone: Meta does not offer ethnicity targeting, and many bilingual buyers use the app in English. Instead, run Spanish, English and bilingual creative against the same broad audience, keep the language consistent after the click, and keep the version with the lowest cost per paying customer.

To reach US Hispanic customers with Meta ads, stop looking for the perfect audience setting and start testing language and creative against the number that pays the bills: cost per paying customer. Meta does not offer ethnicity targeting, and a Spanish language setting leaves out many bilingual buyers who use Facebook and Instagram in English. What works is a structured test of Spanish, English and bilingual ads, with the same language carried through the whole path to purchase.

This guide shows how we set up that test, how to budget it and how to read the results.

Why there is no "Hispanic" audience on Meta

Meta removed detailed targeting options that reference sensitive topics, including race and ethnicity, starting January 19, 2022. Ads for housing, employment and credit carry additional targeting restrictions in the US. If you sell loans, credit cards or real estate, plan for even fewer audience controls.

What remains useful:

  • Location. States, metro areas and ZIP codes where your customers live and where you can deliver.
  • Languages. Meta lets you narrow an audience by language and also run ads in multiple languages inside one campaign.
  • Your own data. Custom audiences from customers and leads, and lookalikes built from your best buyers.

That list is shorter than most briefs assume. The rest of the job falls on the ad itself.

The language setting trap

Adding "Spanish" as a language looks like the obvious shortcut. It has a blind spot: a bilingual customer who set up their phone and their apps in English may not match that setting, even if a Spanish ad would persuade them faster. Narrowing by language can shrink your audience to Spanish-dominant users and hide the bilingual segment, which may include many of the buyers you want.

So treat the language setting as one test variable, not as the definition of the market. Let the creative do the selecting: a Spanish hook, a familiar setting or a culturally specific offer tells the algorithm who responds, and the algorithm learns from purchases, not from your assumptions.

How to set up Meta ads for US Hispanic customers: the three-version test

We run the first round as three versions of the same offer, each in its own ad set with the same budget, the same location and the same optimization event:

VersionCreativeAudience settingWhat it tells you
AEnglishBroad, no language filterYour baseline CAC
BSpanish, written natively (not translated)Broad, no language filterWhether Spanish creative finds cheaper buyers on its own
CSpanish or bilingualNarrowed to Spanish languageWhether the language filter helps or only shrinks reach

Rules that keep the test honest:

  1. One offer, three languages. If the Spanish version also has a different discount, you are testing the discount, not the language.
  2. Optimize for the event that pays. Purchases or qualified leads, never clicks. Meta optimizes toward whatever event you choose.
  3. Same budget, same dates. Run the versions in parallel so seasonality and auction prices affect them equally.
  4. Track each customer back to its version. Your CRM or checkout must record the campaign and ad set; otherwise CAC per version is a guess.

Keep the language after the click

The most common reason a Spanish ad "does not work" has nothing to do with the ad. The person clicks, lands on an English-only page, fills out an English form and gets a call from someone who does not speak Spanish. Each switch loses buyers you already paid to reach.

Before you judge version B or C, check the whole path:

  • Landing page in the same language as the ad, with prices, terms and the call to action translated, not just the headline.
  • Forms with Spanish labels and error messages.
  • First response in minutes, in Spanish. An automated first reply on WhatsApp or by SMS can qualify the lead and hand it to a Spanish-speaking closer; our automation work does exactly that.
  • Sales and support that can continue the conversation in Spanish through to payment.

If one of those links is missing, fix it first. Otherwise you will conclude that Spanish ads are expensive when the leak is downstream.

Budget the test from your maximum CAC

A test needs enough paying customers per version to tell a real difference from noise. Work it backwards from your unit economics.

Step 1: maximum CAC. Suppose an average order of $150, a 40% gross margin and two orders per year. Each customer generates $150 × 40% × 2 = $120 of gross profit per year. If you are willing to invest half of that to acquire them, your maximum CAC is $60.

Step 2: customers per version. Decide how many customers each version needs before you trust it. Twenty per version is a reasonable floor for a first read; more is better for close results.

Step 3: test budget. Versions × customers per version × maximum CAC = 3 × 20 × $60 = $3,600 as the most the round should cost. If a version is clearly above the maximum CAC well before it reaches 20 customers, pause it and move its budget to the others.

These are round numbers to show the arithmetic. Use your own order value, margin and repeat rate.

Read the results with total CAC, not media CAC

A Spanish version can win on ad spend and still lose on total cost, or the opposite. Compare total CAC per version:

Total CAC = (ad spend + sales and service cost for that version) ÷ new paying customers

As a worked example: if version B spent $1,200 and needed $300 of extra Spanish-speaking sales time to close its customers, its total cost is $1,500. Divide by the customers it actually produced and compare that figure with version A calculated the same way. Then look one level deeper:

  • ARPU by version. If Spanish-speaking customers buy more often or choose larger plans, a slightly higher CAC can still be the better business.
  • Payback. Months until gross profit from a customer covers their CAC. A shorter payback lets you scale with less cash at risk.

This is why we build paid media reports with the client's finance team: the winning version is the one that improves CAC, revenue-generating users and ARPU together, not the one with the cheapest click.

Common mistakes

  • Translating instead of writing. A literal translation of an English hook often sounds stiff. Native writers, real testimonials and settings your customers recognize do more than a perfect translation.
  • Treating "Hispanic" as one market. Origin, generation and region change tone, references and even word choice. Once a language wins, test messages by state or metro area.
  • Judging after a few days. Early numbers swing. Decide on customers, not on the first 48 hours of clicks.
  • Too few creatives. One ad per version tests that ad, not the language. Run at least two or three hooks per version; AI UGC makes that volume affordable.
  • Ignoring special ad categories. If your product falls under credit, housing or employment, set it up correctly from day one so the campaign is not rejected mid-test.

A one-page checklist

QuestionIf the answer is no
Do we know our maximum CAC?Calculate it from order value, margin and repeat rate
Is each version optimized for purchases or qualified leads?Change the optimization event
Does the landing page match the ad's language?Translate the full page, not just the headline
Do Spanish leads get a reply in Spanish within minutes?Automate the first response and route to a Spanish speaker
Can we see customers and revenue by version?Fix CRM attribution before scaling

The bottom line

Reaching US Hispanic customers on Meta is not an audience setting; it is a test. Run English, Spanish and bilingual versions of the same offer, keep the language consistent all the way to payment, budget the round from your maximum CAC and keep the version with the lowest total cost per paying customer.

Frequently asked questions

Can you target Hispanic people on Facebook and Instagram?

Not by ethnicity. Meta removed detailed targeting options tied to sensitive topics such as race and ethnicity in 2022. You can still narrow by location and language, but the practical way to reach US Hispanic customers is through creative, language and offer, letting the algorithm find the people who respond and judging the result by cost per paying customer.

Should my Meta ads for US Hispanic customers be in Spanish or English?

There is no single answer, because the US Hispanic market includes Spanish-dominant, bilingual and English-dominant customers. Test Spanish, English and bilingual versions with the same offer and budget, then compare cost per paying customer, not cost per click. Many brands end up running more than one language at the same time.

How much budget do I need to test Spanish vs English Meta ads?

Work backwards from your maximum CAC. Multiply the number of test versions by the customers you need per version to decide, and by your maximum CAC. With three versions, 20 customers each and a $60 maximum CAC, the test can cost up to $3,600 before you have a clear winner.

Is translating my English ads into Spanish enough?

Usually not. A literal translation keeps the English idea but loses the tone, the cultural reference and sometimes the clarity of the offer. Write the Spanish version as its own ad, ideally with native speakers, and make sure the landing page, WhatsApp replies and sales calls continue in the same language.

Does Click-to-WhatsApp work for US Hispanic customers?

It is worth testing when your customers already use WhatsApp and you can answer within minutes in Spanish. Judge it the same way as any other path: cost per conversation is only a diagnostic, and the number that decides is how many conversations become paying customers and at what total cost.
